name: bpftime
baseline: Linux kernel uprobe/uretprobe (the in-kernel dynamic instrumentation path used by perf probe, bpftrace and bcc)
workload: Per-hit latency of an instrumented empty function (__bench_uprobe, __bench_uretprobe, both) with a uprobe/uretprobe attached, kernel eBPF uprobe versus bpftime userspace runtime.
claimed_speedup: README: up to 10x lower uprobe overhead than kernel uprobe/uretprobe. Generated benchmark table: uprobe 2561.57 ns kernel vs 190.02 ns userspace (13.48x); uretprobe 3019.45 ns vs 187.10 ns (16.14x); uprobe+uretprobe 3119.28 ns vs 191.63 ns (16.28x).
hardware: Intel Core Ultra 7 258V (4 cores, 4 threads), 15.07 GB RAM, Linux 6.11.0-24-generic (results generated 2025-04-30)
tradeoffs: Runs eBPF programs in userspace via LD_PRELOAD or a daemon, so it only sees processes it is injected into; no kernel-wide view; needs its own verifier (PREVAIL) or the kernel verifier; kernel baseline requires root and a recent kernel.
caveats: Compiler and flags are not stated on the benchmark page. Kernel uprobe is not one of the listed baselines (perf, gprof, Valgrind) though perf probe and bpftrace use it. Microbenchmark of an empty probed function; real workload speedups are smaller (README says up to 10x; table shows 13-16x). Peer-reviewed paper (OSDI 2025) is cited in the README but was not opened (venue blocked). Not a sampling profiler; it is an instrumentation runtime.
found_via: WebSearch: userspace tracing instrumentation framework faster than uprobe; github.com/topics/instrumentation?l=c++

name: Tracy Profiler
baseline: uninstrumented run of the same program (no profiler); manual positions it against sampling profilers such as perf, VTune and Very Sleepy but gives no head-to-head numbers
workload: Cost of one instrumented zone (start plus end event) measured on the etcpak ETC1/ETC2 block compressor, 16384x16384 image, 12 threads, 16,777,216 zones per image.
claimed_speedup: Profiling adds only 2.25 ns per zone: ETC1 110.9 ms clean vs 148.2 ms profiled (+37.3 ms), ETC2 212.4 ms vs 250.5 ms (+38.1 ms); average difference 37.7 ms over 16,777,216 zones.
tradeoffs: Needs manual zone markup for the headline numbers (sampling and automated instrumentation cost more); GPU/CPU client plus separate server GUI; per-zone cost depends on rdtsc and TLS queue; must profile on bare metal.
caveats: Does not beat a named competing profiler: the number is its own overhead versus an unprofiled run, so it only weakly meets the baseline rule. CPU model and compiler flags are not stated in the manual section. Include only if the orchestrator wants the category incumbent listed. Third-party blog figures (about 15 ns per zone, Optick 30-60 ns, Remotery 50-100 ns) were seen only as search snippets and are not used.
found_via: Starting query C++ frame profiler nanosecond overhead Tracy benchmark; manual/tracy.tex section 'Performance impact'

name: Palanteer
baseline: spdlog (for its logging component); profiling events have no named baseline
workload: Runtime cost and compile cost of a printf-style log call versus spdlog and Nanolog; separately about 25 ns per recorded profiling event on a standard x64 machine.
claimed_speedup: README: logging is ~50x faster at runtime than spdlog and only twice slower than Nanolog; 6x faster to compile a log call than spdlog and 10x faster than Nanolog; ~25 ns cost per event.
license: MIT (instrumentation libraries); AGPL-3.0-or-later (viewer and Python scripting module)
tradeoffs: Beta state, evolving protocol and storage formats; client libraries MIT but viewer is AGPL; instrumentation is manual or Python-automatic.
caveats: The comparison is an internal one linked to a project page that could not be opened (github.io blocked), so only the README summary numbers are recorded. The spdlog/Nanolog comparison concerns the logging feature, not profiling, and spdlog is not a listed baseline for this category; may belong in a logging category. No benchmark code, compiler, flags or CPU stated on the README.
found_via: github.com/topics/profiler?l=c++ (sorted by stars); README performance section
